title: Shares: Meaning, Types and Methods of Issue
summary: What a share is, the types of share, and the five methods of issuing shares, including the two meanings of 'offer for sale'.

p: A share is a unit of ownership in a company. A company issues shares to get capital for starting, expanding or financing special projects, without borrowing. Shares are bought by the public or by existing shareholders. The issue of shares is governed by CAMA. Shares may be issued for cash or for something else of value, such as land, equipment or services (non-cash consideration).

Ordinary shares: carry voting rights; the dividend depends on profit, so it can be large or nothing; ordinary shareholders are the real owners and carry the most risk. Preference shares: paid a fixed dividend before ordinary shareholders and repaid first if the company is wound up; usually without a vote. Deferred shares: dividends only after all other shares have been paid. Redeemable shares: shares that the company can buy back at an agreed time.
Study the table.

1. Offer for subscription (public issue): the company invites the public to apply for shares through a prospectus. Applicants send money with their applications; the company allots shares. Used when large sums are needed.

2. Offer for sale: the company (or its existing shareholders) sells shares to an issuing house, which then sells them to the public. The company avoids the work of dealing with many applicants. Careful: if the sellers are existing shareholders, the company gets no new money, only the ownership changes hands; if the company itself sells to the issuing house, the company does receive the money.

3. Rights issue: existing shareholders are offered new shares in proportion to what they already hold, often at a price below the market price. It raises money and keeps control with the present owners.
4. Private placement: shares are sold to chosen investors or institutions, not to the public. It is quicker and cheaper, with fewer rules.
5. Bonus (scrip) issue: free shares given to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings. No money comes in. It changes reserves into share capital.
The note says 'Right Issue'. The correct term is rights issue (more than one right).

title: Issuing Shares for Cash: Steps and Journal Entries
summary: The steps of an issue for cash and the six journal entries for application, allotment and call, with a worked example.

p: 1. Authorisation: the Articles must allow the issue. 2. Prospectus or offer document: published if the shares are offered to the public. 3. Application: investors apply and send application money. 4. Allotment: the directors decide how many shares to give each applicant. 5. Calls: the company may ask for the rest of the money in instalments.

XYZ Plc issues 100,000 ordinary shares of ₦1 each at par, payable 50 kobo on application, 30 kobo on allotment and 20 kobo on the final call. Total capital = 100,000 × ₦1 = ₦100,000. Application = 100,000 × 0.50 = ₦50,000. Allotment = 100,000 × 0.30 = ₦30,000. Final call = 100,000 × 0.20 = ₦20,000.
Each instalment goes through a temporary account (Application, Allotment or Call) and is then moved to Share Capital.

Allotment and calls are due on a date; the company can see who has paid and who has not (calls in arrears). If an applicant is refused shares, the application money is refunded from the application account. After all the transfers, the Share Capital account shows ₦100,000, the full value of shares issued.

If shares of ₦1 are sold for ₦1.20, the extra 20 kobo is a share premium. It is credited to a Share Premium Account (not Share Capital). The premium is part of the money the company receives, but it is not part of the nominal capital.

title: Over-subscription and Under-subscription, with a Worked Assignment
summary: What happens when applications exceed or fall short of the shares offered, and the full solution to the XYZ Plc assignment.

p: Over-subscription happens when the public applies for more shares than the company offers. The directors can give shares to some applicants and refuse others, or give each applicant a part of what he or she asked for (a pro-rata allotment). The extra application money is either refunded or kept and used to pay the allotment due.

Under-subscription happens when applications are fewer than the shares offered. If the shares subscribed are fewer than the minimum subscription fixed by law, the issue fails and all money is refunded. Often an underwriter (a financial institution) agrees to buy the shares that the public does not.

XYZ Plc offered 80,000 shares of ₦2 each, payable ₦1 on application and ₦1 on allotment. Applications were received for 100,000 shares. The directors allotted shares pro rata to all applicants, and the surplus application money was applied to allotment.
Step 1: money received on application = 100,000 × ₦1 = ₦100,000.
Step 2: shares allotted 80,000. Pro rata means 80,000 ÷ 100,000 = 4 shares for every 5 applied for. Application money needed for 80,000 shares = 80,000 × ₦1 = ₦80,000.
Step 3: surplus application money = 100,000 – 80,000 = ₦20,000, applied to allotment.
Step 4: allotment due = 80,000 × ₦1 = ₦80,000. Less surplus 20,000. Cash to be received on allotment = ₦60,000.
Study the table.

Share Application account: debit 100,000 (transfers: 80,000 to Share Capital and 20,000 to Share Allotment); credit 100,000 from the bank. It balances at zero. Share Allotment account: debit 80,000; credits 20,000 (from application) and 60,000 (bank). It also balances at zero. Share Capital account: credit 160,000 (80,000 shares × ₦2). Bank: debit 100,000 + 60,000 = 160,000.
If the directors reject some applications completely, the application money of those applicants is refunded: Dr Share Application, Cr Bank. Then the rest is allotted in the usual way.

title: Loan Capital: Meaning, Features and Types
summary: What loan capital is, its features and types (debentures, bonds, term loans, mortgages) and how it differs from share capital.

p: Loan capital is money borrowed by a company from outside (individuals, banks or other institutions). It must be repaid on an agreed date with interest. Unlike share capital, it gives the lender no ownership. It is normally used for long-term finance and comes as debentures, bonds, term loans or mortgages.

It is a debt: it must be repaid whether the company makes a profit or a loss. Interest is fixed or variable and paid at agreed times. Lenders are not owners and usually have no vote. In liquidation, lenders are paid before shareholders. It has a fixed term, for example 5, 10 or 15 years. It may be secured on the company's assets or unsecured.

Debentures: a written acknowledgement of a debt issued by the company, usually under its seal; secured or unsecured; redeemable or irredeemable; interest is paid whatever the profits. Bonds: like debentures, often used for government or large company borrowing; can be traded in the capital market. Term loans: borrowed from banks or other institutions for a fixed time and repaid by instalments or at the end. Mortgages: long-term loans secured on land or buildings.

title: Accounting for Loan Capital and Interest
summary: The journal entries when a loan is received, interest is paid and the loan is repaid, with the solutions to the questions.

p: A company borrows ₦1,000,000 from a bank at 10% a year for 5 years. Entry: Dr Bank ₦1,000,000; Cr Loan payable (a long-term liability) ₦1,000,000. (Being a loan received from the bank.)

Yearly interest = ₦1,000,000 × 10% = ₦100,000. Entry: Dr Interest expense ₦100,000; Cr Bank ₦100,000. The interest expense is charged to the Profit and Loss Account for the year (it reduces profit). If the interest is not yet paid at the year end, it is an accrued expense: Dr Interest expense, Cr Accrued interest (a current liability).
Dr Loan payable; Cr Bank for the amount repaid. If the loan is repaid in instalments, the part that falls due within a year is a current liability and the rest remains long term.

When a company issues ₦500,000 of 12% debentures at par: Dr Bank 500,000; Cr Debentures 500,000. Yearly interest = 12% × 500,000 = ₦60,000 (Dr Debenture interest, Cr Bank). In the balance sheet, debentures are shown as a non-current liability (long-term loan).
Evaluation 5: ₦500,000 at 12% gives interest ₦60,000 for one year.
Assignment 3: ₦2,000,000 of bonds at 8% gives interest ₦160,000 a year.

Debenture holders and shareholders: debenture holders are lenders; they get fixed interest which must be paid even if there is no profit; they are paid before shareholders in liquidation and have no vote. Shareholders are owners; they get dividends only if profit is made and vote at meetings.
Two risks of too much borrowing: (1) interest and repayments must be paid even in a bad year, so the company may fail; (2) lenders may take the secured assets if the company defaults.

sections.h: Interest for part of a year
p: If ₦1,000,000 is borrowed on 1 October at 10% a year, the interest for the three months to 31 December is 1,000,000 × 10% × 3/12 = ₦25,000.

title: Second Term Revision: Companies, Shares and Loans
summary: A checklist for the term with the key differences, the CAMA reminders and the answers to the main assignments.

p: Formation of a company: stages and documents. Private and public companies, and quoted and unquoted companies. The financial system: institutions, markets, instruments, laws, functions. Issue of shares: types, methods, journals, over- and under-subscription. Loan capital: types, features, accounting.

Seven people who want to sell shares to the public: a public company (Plc), because only a public company can invite the public to buy shares. A company raising capital quickly by selling ownership to the public: it should become a public (and preferably quoted) company; benefits: large capital, liquidity, credibility. Journal entries for three-instalment issue: see the XYZ Plc table. XYZ Plc assignment: cash on application ₦100,000; surplus ₦20,000; cash on allotment ₦60,000; share capital ₦160,000. Loan interest: ₦60,000 and ₦160,000.

CAMA 2020 allows a private company with one member and requires a public company to have at least two. Minimum issued share capital: ₦100,000 for a private and ₦2,000,000 for a public company. The older figures (2 or 7 members; maximum 50 for a private company) and a separate certificate of commencement appear in older textbooks, so use them only if your examiner expects them.
